60.0.0.en: 1- “O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast broken us down, thou hast been displeased; O turn us again.”

60.0.2.en: 1- David reproaches God because He cast off His children and broke them down, that is, entered among the ranks of the army, divided it and scattered it. He was also displeased with it, that is, disciplined it with severe anger. All this shows God’s forsaking of His people, so they were exposed to the violence of the enemy armies. But David’s faith and his hope in God appear in his saying “turn us again,” that is, return Your care to us, and let us return to Your embrace, that You may shepherd us with Your fatherhood and love.

60.0.3.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about what happened in the Assyrian captivity and then the Babylonian, when God forsook His people and disciplined them with captivity, and the enemies broke into them, ruined their land and took them as slaves. But the people of God repented, put away the idols and lusts, and asked Him to bring them back from captivity, and He restored them with great honor, and they built the Temple.

60.0.4.en: 3- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, who was rejected and broken in upon, and on whom the divine displeasure came in the sufferings and the Cross for our sake, because He bore the sins of the whole world, but He returns with power in the holy Resurrection.

60.1.0.en: 2- “Thou hast made the earth to tremble; thou hast broken it: heal the breaches thereof; for it shaketh.”

60.1.1.en: Broken it: split it and divided it.

60.1.2.en: 1- David shows what happened to his army when he was fighting the Arameans, and likens what happened to an earthquake that split the ground under their feet, so the enemies attacked them, and therefore he asks God to mend the breach that occurred in the army; God answered, and he overcame the Arameans, and also the Edomites in the south.

60.1.3.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about what happened to Jerusalem in the Babylonian attack, which he likens to an earthquake that split the land and shook it, and he asks God to mend its breach, and this is what happened when God brought His people back from captivity, and they built the Temple and worshiped God in it.

60.1.4.en: 3- This is a prophecy about the crucified Christ, at whose crucifixion the earth shook, but He rose and brought calm back to the souls that believed in Him, so they lived in peace, and He mended every weakness in them.

60.2.0.en: 3- “Thou hast shewed thy people hard things: thou hast made us to drink the wine of staggering.”

60.2.2.en: Staggering: swaying and shaking as happens to one who is drunk with wine.

60.2.3.en: 1- What happened to the army of the children of Israel before Aram David describes as hard things, and likens it to intoxicating wine, which makes the one who drinks it stagger, that is, the army of the children of Israel became weak before Aram, but when God was sought it regained its strength and defeated the enemies, and even defeated Edom, which took advantage of the opportunity and attacked the south of the land of the Jews.

60.2.4.en: 2- This hardship and wine of staggering is what has happened to Christians from the beginning of the apostolic age until today, but God does not leave His people who cry out to Him in repentance.

60.3.0.en: 4- “Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth. Selah.”

60.3.1.en: 1- Here David shows God’s answer to the cry of His people, whom He had disciplined and who returned to Him; then God had compassion on His people who fear Him and gave them a banner, the banner of victory, for it was customary in ancient wars for armies to raise a banner of victory. This banner is raised to proclaim the truth, who is God, the supporter of His people, so that He defeats their enemies.

60.3.2.en: 2- The first banner that God gave to His people to reassure them was the rainbow, to confirm to them that He would not flood the world with a deluge again, and this banner is still raised today when the rain comes down heavily.

60.3.3.en: 3- The people of God in Egypt in the days of Moses raised the banner over their houses, which was the blood with which they smeared the upper doorpost and the two side posts when they slaughtered the lamb, and the destroying angel passed over their houses, because they were under the protection of the blood, which signifies the blood of Christ.

60.3.4.en: 4- In the war with Satan the banner is the crucified Christ, who is the truth, who bound Satan by the Cross; our banner is the Cross. The Church confirms this verse in the Friday psali.

60.3.5.en: 5- The word Selah is a musical pause for meditating on the power of God that He gives to those who fear Him, who love the truth.

60.4.0.en: 5- “That thy beloved may be delivered; save with thy right hand, and hear me.”

60.4.1.en: 1- The banner of victory that God gave to His beloved, His children and those who fear Him, delivers them from the hands of the enemies, and they are saved from every tribulation by the power of God, that is, His right hand, so David rejoices, because God answered his prayers and delivered his people.

60.4.2.en: 2- David here asks for his people and not only for himself, for he feels his responsibility and fatherhood toward all his people, so he prays for them that God may give them complete victory, because God’s right hand is able to do all things.

60.4.3.en: Take care to pray for everyone around you, for you are responsible for them before God to guide them and encourage them in their relationship with God, and if you cannot speak, at least lift up your prayers, and be an example to them.

60.5.s.en: (2) Joy in the victory of God

60.5.0.en: 6- “God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth.”

60.5.1.en: Shechem: a city lying west of the Jordan River, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, now called Nablus, in which Jacob dwelt in ancient times.

60.5.2.en: Succoth: a region lying east of the Jordan River, south of the Jabbok River, in which Jacob dwelt in ancient times.

60.5.3.en: 1- God commanded by His holy word and promised David to give him the whole kingdom of Israel, which dwells east and west of the Jordan River, that is, the land of Canaan and everything around it. And God rejoices and is glad at this, and divides the land and measures its borders and gives it all to His people over whom David reigns.

60.5.4.en: 2- These words apply also to David, who rejoices in God’s promise to him, and so possesses the land east and west of the Jordan River, and the nations around him submit to him. This land is where the first fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob dwelt and blessed it.

60.5.5.en: 3- God in the fullness of time spoke by His holy Son, who became incarnate for our redemption. And God is glad because His Son is the object of His pleasure. And He divides and measures the land, which signifies the blessings of the New Testament given in His Church in the form of the Holy Sacraments, the means of grace, and the fruits and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

60.6.0.en: 7- “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the helmet of my head; Judah is my scepter.”

60.6.1.en: Gilead: the grandson of Manasseh, a wide region lying east of the Jordan River, in which half the tribe of Manasseh dwelt.

60.6.2.en: Ephraim: the largest of the tribes in the northern kingdom of Israel, and its first line of defense. Judah: the tribe from which King David came, and whose descendants continued to reign over this tribe until Christ came from his descendants.

60.6.3.en: My scepter: the golden staff that the king holds, which represents his authority and his kingship.

60.6.4.en: 1- God declares that He has the region east of the Jordan, which is Gilead, where half the tribe of Manasseh dwelt with the tribes of Reuben and Gad; that is, God settled His people east of the Jordan River, and settled them also west of the Jordan River, where the tribe of Ephraim, large in number, reigned, which held a wide region and represents the great power in the northern kingdom of Israel; therefore He called it my helmet, that is, the protection of my head, for it is the first defender of the kingdom of Israel. As for Judah, it is also a large tribe dwelling in the south west of the Jordan River, and from it came King David and his descendants who reigned over the kingdom of Judah.

60.6.5.en: 2- Though God permitted His people dwelling east of the Jordan, and in the kingdom of Israel, to be taken as slaves in the Assyrian captivity, and the kingdom of Judah also to be taken with the Babylonian captivity, yet they are all His children whom He brings back from captivity and keeps, because they believed in Him and lived with Him.

60.7.0.en: 8- “Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast my shoe: O Philistia, shout thou over me.”

60.7.1.en: Moab: a son of Lot; a people hostile to the people of God, who dwell east of the Dead Sea.

60.7.2.en: Edom: the descendants of Esau; a people hostile to the people of God, who dwell south of the kingdom of Judah.

60.7.3.en: Philistia: a people hostile to the people of God who dwell south-east of the kingdom of Judah.

60.7.4.en: My washpot: a vessel for washing off filth.

60.7.5.en: 1- After David showed God’s grace given to him in possessing the land of Gilead, with the tribe of Manasseh dwelling in it, the strength given to the tribe of Ephraim, and the wisdom given to the tribe of Judah that kings might come out of it, he spoke in this verse about the hostile peoples who resist the children of Israel. And he showed his wishes that Moab become a washpot for him, that is, be brought low, he and his pagan gods, so that the people of God are not drawn to them but despise them. As for Edom, proud in its dwelling in the mountains, it will be brought low, and David and the children of Israel will tread it with their shoes. As for Philistia, which humbled the children of Israel greatly, David will subdue it, so that it shouts over him and cries out in pain at what he will do to it when he triumphs over it.

60.7.6.en: 2- God, who graciously gave His people possession of the land of Canaan and what is around it, also gave His people to overcome the nations around them so that they would not resist them, and this actually happened in the days of David, and then Solomon.

60.7.7.en: If God is with us, who is against us. Do not be troubled by tribulations or threats, but always remember the power of God that is with you, which supports you and even glorifies you and gladdens your heart.

60.8.0.en: 9- “Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom?”

60.8.1.en: When David looked at the capital of the land of Edom, high on the mountains and fortified by them, so that it is very hard to reach and subdue, he cried out to God and said, expressing his weakness, who will lead me to it; and this shows David’s humility and his declaring his need of God, especially before the power of the enemies, that is, Edom.

60.9.0.en: 10- “Is it not thou, O God, who hast cast us off, and goest not forth, O God, with our armies?”

60.9.1.en: David continued his prayer and said to God, there is none but You, O Lord, who brings me to Edom, so that I may triumph over it by Your power, and I know that You cast us off and did not go out with our armies for a time, to discipline us, so that we may trust that the strength is from You and not from us, and so be humbled and repent of our sins.

60.10.0.en: 11- “Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man.” 12- “Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies.” Valiantly: with strength.

60.10.1.en: 1- In conclusion David declares that man is unable to save himself and must need God’s help. Man’s strength appears strong outwardly, but it is temporary and weak before the changes of life. The solution is to take refuge in God and ask His help.

60.10.2.en: 2- David says that if we trust in God, He intervenes with mighty power and defeats our enemies and treads them down, so that they have no strength before us, whether the demons or the wicked who follow them, because God’s power cannot be resisted.

60.10.3.en: Do not be troubled by your helplessness and the weakness of your strength before the demands of life, because your God is able to make up every lack in you, and even supports you so that you become stronger than those around you and distinguished, and so glorify God.

60.10.4.en: Thanksgiving to God the stronghold. To the chief Musician upon stringed instruments. A psalm of David: “Hear my cry, O God; attend unto my prayer” (v. 1) Introduction:

60.10.6.en: 2- When was it written? When he fled from the face of Absalom his son, and then David’s army defeated the army of the children of Israel, and Absalom was killed.

60.10.7.en: 3- This psalm was sung by a group of Levites led by a chief, that is, a leader.

60.10.8.en: 4- The repeating of this psalm is accompanied by a musical instrument called the stringed instrument, an ancient stringed instrument resembling the oud and the rebab.

60.10.9.en: 5- This psalm shows David the man of prayer, the believer, who trusts in God and is full of hope and loves His worship.

60.10.10.en: 6- This psalm is a prophecy about the feelings of the captives before their return from captivity to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the Temple.

60.10.11.en: 7- This psalm is counted among the liturgical psalms, for the congregation of the people of God repeats it in tribulations, and when praying for the king, or the high priest.

60.10.12.en: 8- This psalm is also counted among the Messianic psalms, because it speaks in the spirit of prophecy about Christ the King, who reigns for ever (vv. 6, 7).

60.10.13.en: 9- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, in which Christ offered Himself on the Cross for our salvation; therefore this psalm cries out to God the King to deliver us from all our tribulations, make us steadfast in Him and give us complete salvation.

61.0.s.en: (1) A cry to God the refuge

61.0.0.en: 1- “Hear my cry, O God; attend unto my prayer.” 2- “From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.”

61.0.1.en: Overwhelmed: lost consciousness; here it means weakness, and in the Hebrew original it means suffering and writhing.

61.0.2.en: 1- David felt that he was far from Jerusalem, the holy city, and from the ark of the covenant of God, so he felt isolation and that he was at the end of the earth; therefore he cried out to God with fervent prayers, and hoped that God would hear him, especially since he was in great weakness that overwhelmed his heart and made him suffer severely and writhe, especially as he was isolated and driven out by his son. And he asked God to lead him to a high rock, “higher than I,” and firm, that he might climb upon it, and his faith was that his rock is God and that God would lift him upon this rock, that is, make his faith firm, raise him above all his sorrows and pains and give him assurance and peace; so David was asking God not only for His protection but to raise him above his toils.

61.0.3.en: 2- These two verses are a prophecy about the captives of the Assyrian and Babylonian captivity who pray while far from Jerusalem, scattered in the world and suffering, but their hope is the return to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the Temple, where God is their rock.

61.0.4.en: 3- Christ is the rock who appeared in the Old Testament with Moses, of whom David speaks here, who is the hope of mankind, that is, the Cross that offered salvation to the whole world.

61.1.0.en: 3- “For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy.”

61.1.1.en: 1- David remembers God’s protection of him throughout his former life, and is filled with trust and faith in God, and says, “Thou hast been a shelter for me.” So ought every person to remember God’s former works and thank Him for them, so that his faith grows and is made firm.

61.1.2.en: 2- God was to David not only a shelter but a tower from which he watches the enemy and discovers the hidden and concealed enemies, and strikes them with arrows. So God did not only protect David but gave him strength to attack his enemies, and they feared him. So also the demons fear the holy children of God.

61.1.3.en: 3- Christ is a shelter for His children who protects them from every sin, and He is a strong tower by which they discover all the schemes of the demons, and even attack them with humility, the acquiring of virtues and the doing of good, and He also repels from them the hidden enemies, that is, the demons, and overcomes them.

61.1.4.en: 4- 1- Since David, in his exile from the face of Absalom, was sure that God is his refuge and his strength, he wished to dwell in God’s tabernacle, that is, His Temple, for ever. What is meant, of course, is not to live inside the Holy Place or the Holy of Holies, but to live beside the Temple of God, as the Hebrew original of the word means, so that he could offer continual worship to God. Indeed, out of his love for the house of God he wished to dwell in his heart, that is, to enjoy God’s dwelling in him throughout his life.

61.1.5.en: 2- David wished that God would protect him with the covering of His wings, so that no one could harm him, because God surrounds him with His care and love, as the cherubim spread their wings over the cover of the ark of the covenant of God; therefore the cover was called the mercy seat, and the glory of God appeared on the cover of the ark. That is, David wishes to receive God’s mercies when He overshadows him with His wings.

61.1.6.en: 3- What is meant by God’s dwelling is Jerusalem, where the ark of the covenant of God is, so David wishes to offer the worship of God throughout his life. God’s dwelling is also the heavenly Jerusalem, so David wishes to live for ever with God.

61.1.7.en: 4- The verse ends with the word Selah, a musical pause in which man meditates on God’s love, care and mercy.

61.1.8.en: Do you long to be in the Church so as to enjoy seeing God, be nourished by His Holy Sacraments, and cast all your toils into His embrace, so that your heart is at peace and you walk securely in all your steps?!

61.2.0.en: 5- “For thou, O God, hast heard my vows: thou hast given me the heritage of those that fear thy name.”

61.2.1.en: 1- Since David’s heart was attached to the house of God, he wished in his exile to offer vows to God, and mentioned them in his prayers, and God rejoiced when He heard them because they express David’s longing for the house of God and his faith in God’s power, which is able to bring him back from his exile to Jerusalem. And he reminded God of the blessings He gave to him and to all who fear God, which is the promised land from which his son drove him out, but God is able to bring him back to it. This land is a pledge of the inheritance of eternal life.

61.2.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who offered Himself as a vow for us before the Father, when He said in His intercessory prayer, “For their sakes I sanctify myself” (Jn 17:19), and we respond to Christ’s love and sanctify ourselves to Him throughout our lives; for we have become God’s heritage and His possession in Christ, and so we live for Him, consecrating our hearts on earth, and then enjoy fellowship with Him in the Kingdom for ever.

61.3.0.en: 6- “Thou wilt prolong the king’s life: and his years as many generations.” 7- “He shall abide before God for ever: O prepare mercy and truth, which may preserve him.”

61.3.1.en: 1- By faith David saw that God would bring him back from his exile to his throne in Jerusalem, and so his days and years as king are extended, and he remains seated on his throne before God, and God keeps him, working by mercy and truth, that is, justice, so that he governs his people with uprightness. In addition, he reigns for ever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

61.3.2.en: 2- These two verses are a clear prophecy about Christ the King, who reigns for ever, that is, to eternity, and His rule is by mercy and truth. For He fulfilled divine justice, that is, truth, on the Cross by His death for us, and His mercy appeared in the forgiveness of our sins and the renewal of our life in Him. And when we walk in uprightness and reign over ourselves by controlling our lusts and directing our energy to God, God is glorified in us and reigns through us, and by our being kings we are an extension of His kingdom.

61.4.0.en: 8- “So will I sing praise unto thy name for ever, that I may daily perform my vows.”

61.4.1.en: 1- As a result of God’s works that David mentioned in the previous verses, he thanks God at the close of this psalm, and keeps on thanking Him throughout his life, and even wishes to enter the heavenly Kingdom to continue in this thanksgiving for ever. Thus David moved from the appeal and cry to God because of his need of Him, which he mentioned at the beginning of the psalm, and began to thank Him at the end of the psalm, and even entered into a life of constant thanksgiving.

61.4.2.en: 2- David was not content with thanksgiving but promised to perform his vows that he offered to God while in his exile, and promises to perform them day by day. By this he does not mean only a specific, determined vow, but continual worship of God that he offers every day.

61.4.3.en: If you ask and press upon God to supply your needs and solve your problems, do not forget to thank Him after He intervenes and shows His love for you, because by thanksgiving you delight in His gifts, and your faith and your joy in God grow. Trust in God the Savior. To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun. A psalm of David: “Truly my soul waiteth upon God” (v. 1) Introduction:

61.4.6.en: When David was fleeing from the face of Absalom his son.

61.4.7.en: 3- David wrote this psalm and gave it to a chief of the singers named Jeduthun, who is most likely Ethan the Ezrahite, one of the three chiefs of the singers in David’s days, for he was with Asaph and Heman the Ezrahite (1 Chr 15:17). The name Jeduthun is also found in the title of Psalms (39, 77).

61.4.8.en: 4- This psalm shows David’s courage, his trust and his hope in God; it is an encouraging psalm that supports everyone who passes through distress.

61.4.9.en: 5- This psalm also teaches patience, which controls anger and pride.

61.4.10.en: 6- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
